reply:
My dearest Marie,

The day in Amsterdam was full. I posted my letter and finally saw the second part of the gallery; the old town hall, now the imperial palace, is grand, though I suspect the royal family finds it merely a stopover. I also visited a church with coloured windows that caught the light beautifully. Lunch was a simple affair of fish with Dr. Besseling, a Catholic, which gave us ample time to discuss the state of things here.

I left by diligence at five. The journey is tiring but the air is good. I think of you and the boys in Berlin, especially Karl and Immanuel. Please keep Ludwig’s studies steady; discipline remains the foundation of any true learning. I hope to write again soon. Do not worry about the delay in my letters; the roads are busy.

Your affectionate
Georg

My dearest Marie,

The fish at Besseling’s table was tolerable, if a bit too white for my taste, and the Dutch wine was warm. I paid three guilders for the pleasure, which I find exorbitant for such a meal. Dr. Besseling is a pleasant enough Catholic, though he spoke of the Pope with a reverence I found rather theatrical. I have left Amsterdam for Utrecht by diligence, arriving as the light fails.

I saw the former town hall here, now the imperial palace. It is a grand building, though one cannot help but feel a certain melancholy seeing the scars of Napoleon’s ambition still lingering on the walls. The coloured windows in the church were indeed striking; the light through them had a quality that almost made the stone feel alive. I am tired, my love. The journey has been long and the roads are not as smooth as one hopes. I hope the boys are well and that you have not had any trouble with the household accounts. I shall write again when I can find a quiet hour.

Yours,
G.W.F.

So far, I am happy; my last letter from Amsterdam will be in your hands, my dear! I sent it off early on Saturday, on which day I also saw the second, most varied part of the picture gallery—wonderful pieces among them—and further the former town hall, which Napoleon had had set up as an imperial palace. Setting aside this division of rooms and the furnishings, etc., the building (which the royal family still inhabits when they are in Amsterdam) is the most magnificent conception of a town house that a free, wealthy, art-loving citizenry could have conceived. After visiting a church famous for its colored windows and having lunch with Mr. D. Besseling, at whose place I, because he is a stricter Catholic than my Mr. van Ghert, ate fish both times, but excellent fish, I got on the diligence at 5 o’clock in the evening (on Saturday).

My dearest Marie,

The Kassel post office was crowded, but I secured my place on the diligence to Giessen for tomorrow morning. It is a good thing, too, for the heat has been oppressive, and my head feels rather heavy after the journey. I have just read your letter, which reached me in time to sweeten the evening.

I trust the boys are well-behaved. I must remind you to keep a firm hand on them; freedom is the goal of their education, not its starting point. If they learn to obey now, their own judgment will have weight later. Do not let them think they can dictate terms. The world will not be so gentle with them as you are.

I am tired, so I shall retire early. I hope to reach Giessen before noon. I think of you constantly, even in this dull travel.

Yours faithfully,

G. W. F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

I have secured a seat on the diligence for tomorrow, departing Kassel at six to Giessen, where the road splits for Koblenz. The heat here is oppressive; I paid three Kreuzers for a bottle of water at the post office, which felt like robbery, though the clerk was polite enough. I have been walking the streets to cool off. The town is neat but lacks the grandeur of Berlin. I saw a group of students playing whist in a tavern; their form was poor, but their enthusiasm was loud.

Regarding your last letter: I am well, though my shoes are wearing thin. I think of Karl and Immanuel often. The journey is tiring, but the view from the window is pleasant. Do not worry about my health. I will write again when I reach Giessen.

Yours,
G.W.F.

When I went to the post office again after dinner today, where I also registered for tomorrow’s diligence to Giessen—from there the road branches off from the Frankfurt road toward Coblenz—I received your letter, my dear, and cannot tell you enough what joy it gave me.

My dearest Marie,

I write from Breda, weary but content. This morning I walked four hours in Antwerp with Mr. van Ghert. The churches here rival Ghent’s, filled with life-size marbles and dozens of great canvases by Rubens and van Dyck. It is a sight that stirs the soul, though I confess my legs feel it more than my mind.

We parted there. Van Ghert returns to Brussels to seek your letters and forward them to Amsterdam. I trust you are well, and that Karl and Immanuel are settling into their routines. I think of you constantly, and of the quiet of our home in Berlin. The journey continues, but my heart remains with you.

Give my regards to the household. I shall write again when I have news of your correspondence.

Yours ever,

G.W.F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

We walked four hours in Antwerp this morning with Mr. van Ghert. The churches are packed with life-size marble statues, and one nave held two dozen large paintings by Rubens and van Dyck. I confess the sheer volume was dizzying; I felt less like a student of history and more like a man drowning in oil paint. Van Ghert returned to Brussels to check for your letters and send them to Amsterdam. I hope they are safe.

I am tired, but the air is fine. I do not know what to write about the food, but the wine was decent. I miss your company and the quiet of our rooms in Berlin. The Dutch are polite, but they lack a certain spark. I shall wait for word. Give my love to the boys.

Your husband,
G.W.F.

Finally, the churches were the subject of conversation. The churches, as I said—in Ghent and Antwerp, one must go there if one wishes to see sublime, rich Catholic churches—large, spacious, Gothic, majestic—stained glass windows (the most beautiful I have ever seen are in Brussels); on the columns, marble statues life-sized, placed at some height, otherwise lying or sitting—in the dozens;—paintings by Rubens, van Dyck, and their pupils, large works, wonderful ones among them, two to three dozen in a single church; marble columns, bas-reliefs, grilles, confessionals, half a dozen or a full dozen in the Antwerp church—each adorned with four life-sized, excellent wood-carved images—(I thought of the English greeting in Nuremberg);—the town halls equally peculiarly Gothic. We were on our feet in Antwerp for four hours in the morning;—I have sweated a lot for the past eight days; at Waterloo I thought that it had not been quite as much as the French and the Allies had sweated. In Antwerp I parted from my dear friend Mr. van Ghert; he went back to Brussels with the instruction to inquire whether any letters from you had arrived, and to send them to me in Amsterdam.

My dearest Marie,

We have arrived safely in Brunswick, having endured a night in that green morocco carriage which, despite its plush, felt more like a coffin than a conveyance. The coachman arrangement in Magdeburg proved a fiasco, forcing us into this diligence. I am exhausted, but the mind finds some relief in the museum. We viewed the picture gallery, including the specific painting Schulz mentioned. It possesses a certain quiet dignity, though I confess I am too weary to dissect its aesthetic merits fully. The Englishman slept soundly, to his credit. I shall write to the boys when I can sit down properly. Do not worry; I am merely tired, not ill. The journey continues tomorrow.

Yours affectionately,
Wilhelm

My dearest Marie,

We are in Brunswick, having arrived at five this morning after a diligence ride from Magdeburg. The Englishman proved useless; our hired coachman vanished, so we were forced into a green-morocco diligence. It was stifling, but the pace was good.

We visited the museum this morning. The picture gallery is decent, though I must admit I was only looking for the specific painting Schulz mentioned. It is there, and it is merely competent. I paid two thalers for a mediocre lunch; the meat was dry.

I think of Karl and Immanuel. I hope they are well. I will try to find a better coach for the next leg. The heat here is oppressive.

Yours,
Hegel

But now to the matter. So the arrangement with the Englishman to take a hired coach from Magdeburg here has come to nothing; so we set out on the diligence in Magdeburg on Monday noon — to Brunswick. This route to Cassel is the most common, only one or two miles longer than the one I had in mind as the most direct, — has excellent country roads everywhere and good post coaches; and here I must make amends to the Prussian postal service, against which I was indignant in the last letter because of the other routes; the coach is upholstered, lined with green morocco leather, and so forth. Around 5 o'clock in the morning on Tuesday we arrived in Brunswick. — When the suggestion to go via Brunswick was made, it had occurred to me anyway that Mr. Government Commissioner Schulz had told me about a painting that is located there, and which alone is worth a journey. — We have therefore seen the local museum, especially the painting gallery and therein entirely distinguished and outstanding pieces. The painting that Mr. Government Commissioner had in mind is particularly of entirely peculiar excellence.

My dearest Marie,

I have arrived safely in Magdeburg. The afternoon was agreeable; I inspected the cathedral and its striking apostle statues, then called on General Carnot. Walking the Elbe bank, I watched thirteen Hamburg ships sail in—a fine sight of commerce.

I am staying here until Tuesday noon, when the coach to Kassel departs. An Englishman has hired a coachman for a three-day drive to Kassel, which I hope will keep me company. The journey is slow, but I find the delay pleasant. I have eaten well and taken my snuff.

Do not worry for me. I am in good spirits and looking forward to the final leg. I shall write again from Kassel.

Yours ever,
Georg

My dearest Marie,

I reached Magdeburg at one this afternoon. The heat is oppressive, but I managed a walk by the Elbe. Thirteen Hamburg ships came in; the sight was grand, though the dockworkers were rough. I visited the cathedral to see the cast apostles by Fischer of Nuremberg. They are stiff, lifeless things—nature forced into bronze without breath. I also called on General Carnot. He is a polite man, but his conversation was dry as old bread. We drank wine, decent enough, and I paid two thalers for the meal.

I am told the coach to Kassel leaves Tuesday noon. A coachman arrived this morning to drive an Englishman there in three days; he seems hurried. I hope you and the boys are well. I missed our cards last night. The air is thick here, and my head is heavy. I will write again when I am settled.

Your affectionate
G.W.F. Hegel

The first thing I would have to tell you for a good morning, namely that we arrived here safely, partly follows from this itself; the company were decent people; it got cold at night; yet four woolen body linings or skirts protected me sufficiently, so that I, after having with difficulty peeled myself off again, have remained unharmed. Yesterday at noon at 1 o'clock we arrived here, but it is harder to get out of Magdeburg than to come in. — The activity of Mr. Post President and the Prussian intelligence have not yet cast their eye on the local post coach business, at least insofar as it concerns my interest. Until Tuesday noon only does the — I almost said — coach to Cassel go. The journaliers with which I came is not connected with any further courses. To stay here until Tuesday is far too long. So I resolved first, since tomorrow morning the traveling coach to Erfurt goes, to take my course thither; how nice, to bring Goethe the package, which I would have to send from here, myself and from there to go on along the great highway! — Thereupon I looked at the post coach, but what a cart! and then I would have to drive about 44 miles to Cassel — so I decided to take extra post, but I have to hear that I would be carried on further on the same cart, wagon, under open sky. With this briefly resolved, to return quickly to Berlin and to fetch my traveling coach, and with this well equipped, to pleasantly continue my health journey. With this cheerful thought, to see you dear ones again soon, I then fell asleep and slept very well; yet, you see, not, like Peter, in the sense of staying at home, but on the contrary to travel out thoroughly. The former would otherwise have been no wonder either, for I indeed went on the journey with greater reluctance than I dared to say, and if I had not already received the money, it would have been hard to bring me to it, so necessary it was to me in fact. Besides, I also yesterday afternoon saw what there was to see here; — the famous cathedral — it may be remarkable, because it is a cathedral; — but the whole architecture is not such a good conception as the Nuremberg Gothic churches, and what of artwork is inside, a lot of carved and cast, painted and plastered, is far too bad. The cast apostles by Fischer, the Nuremberger, are not to be compared with the Nurembergers. The subjects have entirely fallen into the craft! The dearest thing I have seen is General Carnot, a lovable old man and Frenchman; it is the famous one; — he took it friendly that I visited him. — Then I strolled on the Elbe, a fleet of 13 Hamburg ships with high-swollen sea sails was coming in (each with two, yet only on one mast), beautiful stream, beautiful immeasurable fertile plains (here fertile, but otherwise between Potsdam and Burg, what we saw by day, quite desolate) — more beautiful the clearest sky. Just now a coachman comes, who has to bring an Englishman, who seems to be a German, to Cassel in 3 days; to him I will attach myself...

My dearest Marie,

I have arrived safely in Kassel. The journey from Brunswick was tedious; our carriage waited at Northeim for hours, so I hired a private chaise through Göttingen to Münden, arriving late. I slept until six this morning and pushed on.

My companion is an Englishman, perhaps twenty-six, returning from Italy to Paris. He speaks little of the country he has just left, but his eyes are tired. He reminds me of the restless youth one sees in Berlin, yet there is a quietness in him now. I find myself watching how he carries himself, noting the difference between the freedom he claims and the discipline he lacks. It is a small lesson in ethics, observed on the road.

The weather is pleasant. I shall dine here tonight and continue tomorrow. Do not worry; I am in good spirits. Give my love to the boys.

Your affectionate husband,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

I arrive in Kassel, weary but intact. The diligence from Brunswick was a misadventure; stuck in Northeim until the evening, I hired a post-chaise through Göttingen to Münden, arriving at ten. I slept until six, then continued here. My fellow traveler, a young Englishman of twenty-five returning from Italy to Paris, is loud, ill-dressed, and speaks of “the sublime” with a vulgarity that makes one’s teeth ache. He is a man without a state, purely accidental.

The food was tolerable, the wine thin. I have paid the driver his due. I think of you and the boys, but mostly I think of the mud on my boots. Tell Karl his father is still alive, if that is of any comfort to him. I shall continue tomorrow.

Yours,
G.W.F.

After having slept through the afternoon; though before that I had seen beautiful gardens, an iron obelisk—70 feet high—erected in memory of the two last Dukes who perished in the war against the French, and in the evening I had seen a bad comedy, we set out again after 10 o’clock on the diligence (though more, according to Wolff’s travesty, on the sloth). The night was beautiful, the stars shone magnificently, — the morning star rose particularly beautifully. Now in the daytime we saw a different physiognomy of nature than before, no longer the barren or fertile plains, — beautiful oak forests, mountains, hills, the gentle slopes covered with fruit fields, the valleys filled with meadows, — in short a homely nature — homely, namely for me, for you yourself, born in half-sand, are in Berlin in the homely element, perhaps in a slightly stronger dose. — So in such a beautiful land we traveled on. With my Englishman, who speaks French, and also some German, I got along very well, he is a young man of 25–26 years, a handsome man, somewhat like the actor Blum, and of such, but better, bearing, good-natured, well-informed, comes from Italy, is going to Paris, to travel from there via Milan to Constantinople, a private person, not too rich — in short as I would also wish for companions in the future. In Nordheim, where we arrived at 3 o’clock in the afternoon (yesterday Wednesday), and the carriage had to wait until about 8 or 9 o’clock in the evening for another, I considered that it would be too uncomfortable for me to spend the third night without a bed and proper sleep; I therefore took extra post — it went first to Göttingen — the scholarly Göttingen; say however only to the dear friend Schulze, that as a proper Berlin professor I did not make much of it, to drive on in 5 minutes, but I did not shake the dust from my feet outside the gate, only because I had not picked any up with them. So I traveled to Münden, where I arrived at 10 o’clock — and slept quietly in bed until 6 o’clock today — and finally here. The road is very charming, Cassel lies very excellently in a wide valley; — the Hercules on Wilhelmshöhe is already visible from several hours away as a peak in the middle of a mountain range. Around Cassel itself it is very beautiful; it has streets — i.e. in one part — in the style of Berlin; the Aue is a layout of approximately the kind of the new garden in Potsdam, beautiful green lawn with healthy varied trees scattered, without any shrubbery, — so transparent everywhere; — it is most charming to walk in it — at the end a beautiful water surface, with hanging willows here and there lining the bank, benches etc., also a house where one can drink coffee in the open air, coffee, i.e. chicory broth; for many days I have only had such, and no coffee to drink, — the whole Brunswick country is covered with fields of this lying root. Tomorrow I will go up to Wilhelmshöhe and into the gallery; today the Englishman has left me in the lurch....

My dearest Marie,

I am writing from The Hague, where the evening air is sharp and the city hums with a lively, French inflection. This morning I made the walk to Scheveningen. To stand at the edge of the North Sea is a profound experience; it is not the gentle, domestic waters of the Rhine, but a vast, indifferent force. One feels small before it, yet strangely grounded in one’s own existence. It is a reminder that nature is not merely a backdrop for our thoughts, but a reality with its own weight and dignity.

Afterward, I spent the afternoon in the Bois and visited the picture gallery, which holds some fine works, though I confess I preferred the company of the French comedies in the evening. The wit is sharp, the acting vigorous. It is a pleasure to see art and life intertwined so openly.

I think of you and the boys in Berlin. Please give my regards to Immanuel. I shall write again soon.

Yours ever,
G.W.F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

The sea at Scheveningen is a flat, grey nothing. I walked an hour through the woods to see it and found only damp sand and the smell of fish. A waste of boots, truly. The picture gallery here is decent, though the light in the afternoon was poor. I paid two guilders for a decent dinner in Delft earlier, which was reasonable.

I sat in the Bois for an hour, watching the Dutch look at me with that peculiar, polite indifference. They are a people of water and trade, lacking that fiery spirit of the South, but they have their order. In the evening, three French comedies. The first was tiresome, the second decent, the third a farce of the lowest kind. I laughed, but mostly from relief that it was over.

Karl writes that his Latin is improving. I hope his discipline holds. Do not worry about the cold; I have brought my best coat. I shall return to Berlin soon.

Your loving,
G.W.F. Hegel

From Breda I continued on by diligence at 10 o’clock in the morning, for three run daily from Antwerp to Amsterdam, all via The Hague, and likewise three in return; — from Brussels to Paris, diligences also run every day, one is in Paris in 36 hours for 25 francs, what a temptation! had it not been so late in the season, and besides — had I had news from you, — could one have resisted such a temptation? Likewise in Rotterdam, here a steamboat goes once a week to London — punctual and infallible, unless there is very bad storm — in 24 hours. But now from Breda it went on yesterday without a break, — fertile land, but entirely now on brick-paved roads, like the sidewalk in Berlin — to Mordyk, from there by steamboat across a bay of the sea, the Holland Diep, 1/2 hour wide — my dear friend, the southwest, which had brought me such fine weather for so long, also helped with the better crossing; here ships came from afar, a proud three-masted ship, like a Sultan: majestic white turban, equally swollen white middle garment, then a white, wider lower garment, and a cloak behind, as the figure shows?). From here to Dordrecht, — large seaport, forty, or God knows how many thousand inhabitants; — from here in true Holland, — all houses of reddish bricks, with white lines as if made with a ruler, no edge, no corner crumbled or blunted, — beautiful canals, planted with trees, running through the city, everything full of large ships, the straight beautiful quays everywhere; — then again after 3 o’clock across the wide Meuse; then at 5 o’clock in Rotterdam; what a large city again! then through Delft and after half an hour into beautiful The Hague. The Hague is in fact a village — everywhere beautiful green meadows, so from Dordrecht on! The cleanest vegetable gardens, as nicely kept as Mrs. Voß can keep them, interrupted by rows of trees and cut off from the highway, next to which a canal always runs, and from each other, — cattle everywhere on them, — all black- and white-spotted, they also stay on the meadow at night, one sees people in the evening milking the cows; one travels among all the Potters and Berghems. — This morning out of the gate into a forest, like the Berlin Zoo, only more beautiful alleys of beeches and oaks, no undergrowth — all high and leafy forest; — one hour to Scheveningen, here I saw the unbounded North Sea, the German Sea — my friend the southwest blew strongly and brought the most beautiful waves. — Then I saw the gallery, afternoon strolled in the beautiful woods, more beautiful than the Aue near Cassel, splendid water pieces like in Charlottenburg; — then also once a French comedy and indeed three in one evening seen; I had to rest, for I have walked and stood a lot; — in the gallery is a Württemberg inspector, — beautiful, very beautiful things. — I have today before the mirror tied my neckerchief and seen that I, as I believe, have become thinner, for I have had many fatigues, — but I am otherwise healthy and vigorous and well; also with the money it is still going well, — I have lost, I believe, also nothing yet, and I am almost annoyed about it, for in something one must have bad luck, — but I calculate that I pay for everything in that I have no letters from you

My dearest Marie,

I have arrived in Hamburg, though not yet in our arms. The ship brought me here at ten, but the journey home is blocked. I received your two letters, a welcome relief to my solitary mind, and have sent my luggage to the post office for the express coach. Yet, alas, no seats remain for Wednesday. I am confined to the König von Hannover inn, waiting for Monday’s post wagon, which will finally bring me to Berlin by Thursday.

The delay is a minor inconvenience, but the thought of your letters keeps my spirits high. I trust Karl and Immanuel are well, and that you are managing the household without too much strain. I am in good health, if somewhat weary from the sea air. I shall wait these days with patience, for freedom is the end of all striving, even that of a man waiting for a carriage.

Give my love to the boys.

Yours,
G. W. F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

I arrived in Hamburg at ten this morning. The heat was oppressive, and the boat ride from Cuxhaven felt less like travel and more like being marinated in brine. I found no passage for today’s express coach, nor even for Wednesday. I am lodged at the König von Hannover, a tolerable house, though the rooms are damp and the beer tastes of tar.

Your two letters waited for me at the post office. I read them by the window, watching the cranes load timber. I was relieved to hear of Karl’s progress, though I suspect Immanuel is still resisting the arithmetic. I must stay here until Monday’s post wagon, arriving Thursday. It is a long wait, but I shall not complain. The city is busy, the air thick, and I have already spent three thalers on a lunch that was barely worth the effort.

I miss your snuff and your sharp tongue. Write when you can.

Yours,
G.W.F.

I have just arrived, and am having my things sent from the ship to the post office, in order to catch the express post today and be with you on Monday; — there is no more space available, not even on Wednesday, but as compensation I find two dear letters from you; how relieved and delighted I am by these good news from you.... I am sitting here in the King of Hanover — before the most beautiful view. — But now I can only depart on Monday by the post coach, which has given me a sense of apprehension, and will not arrive until Thursday.

My dearest Marie,

I arrived at Töplitz this evening, lodging at the new inn under the sign of the King of Prussia. The heat was oppressive during the journey from Abersau, but the change of air here is already refreshing. I followed Fräulein Stok’s advice and climbed the Schlackenberg opposite the inn; the view is striking, though my legs are tired. I have drunk the waters in the Spitalgarten and walked in the park of Prince Clary’s castle. The air is cool, and the water bath (Steinbad) did wonders for my stiff joints. I dined well, and for once, I did not feel the need to argue with my companions over the quality of the wine.

The journey has been long, and I am weary, but the prospect of rest here is a pleasure. I think of you and the boys in Berlin, and I hope this trip will restore my health so that I may return to my work with renewed vigor. Give my love to Karl and Immanuel.

Your affectionate husband,
G. W. F.

My dearest Marie,

The road from Abersau was tedious, but Töplitz is a strange place. I lodged at the *König von Preussen*, a new house, and the room is cool, which I prefer to the stifling heat of the spa. I climbed the Schlackenberg as Fräulein Stok advised; the view is adequate, the air sharp. I drank the waters in the Spitalgarten—they taste of iron and regret, but I swallowed them for the sake of the routine. Later, I strolled Prince Clary’s park, which is overgrown and lacks the discipline of a Berlin garden, and took the Steinbad. It was hot, as stones are.

Dinner was serviceable. A roast duck, heavy but acceptable, and a local white wine that lacked backbone. I paid twelve kreuzer for a glass. The people here are polite but shallow, all talking of cures and carriage rides. I think of you and the boys in the quiet of the evening. The world outside is loud, but here, in the water, one’s thoughts settle. I shall write again soon.

Your husband,
G.W.F.

Order, and they also want nothing better than that one gets along with them in order. From here it goes over Abersau), Culm — the region of the Battle of Culm, through nothing but a succession of hills and fields — all cultivated and fertile — to Töplitz, which lies very beautifully and pleasantly. I lodged in a brand-new inn (one), because its sign is to the King of Prussia. — Today immediately to the Schlackenberg, which is opposite the inn, — Miss Stok had also recommended this route to me, — on this hill one overlooks the entire region around Töplitz, i.e. if one goes around the top of the hill; — an extremely pleasant view, — the very wide region — finally bounded by higher mountain ranges, — the most varied succession of hills, valleys, rows of houses — everything is most cheerful; — then drank the spring water in the hospital garden — one spring is eye-water, which did me great good — into the park, which belongs to the palace of Prince Clary, the lord of the region — then took a bath in the stone bath — a magnificent spring — then dined with appetite — I shall drive to the castle hill. —

My dearest Marie,

The rain has not spared Vienna, and I arrived at the theater late, having neglected the unusual starting time. I missed the opening chorus honoring our good Emperor Franz, which is a pity, though one learns to make the best of it. I did, however, catch the first act of Zelmira. The singing was competent, though I confess the recitative by Donzelli lacked a certain weight. One hears so much in these provinces, yet the spirit of the place remains distinct.

I think of you and the boys in our warm Berlin rooms. The cold here is sharp, but my spirits are not. I hope Ludwig is well and that Karl and Immanuel are applying themselves to their studies with the diligence you so rightly demand of them. Do not worry about me; I am merely a traveler, observing the world as it turns.

Yours ever,
Georg

My dearest Marie,

The weather turned foul on Sunday, and I, in my usual haste, overlooked the early start at the Hofoper. I arrived at seven, far too late for the opening chorus in praise of Franz. A minor tragedy, but I made the best of it. We heard the first act of *Zelmira*. Dardanelli was decent, but Lablache was a bore. Donzelli, however, sang a recitative that was quite exquisite—pure, clear, and without affectation. I paid six florins for a good seat, which I consider fair for the evening’s entertainment.

The food at the theatre was mediocre, as usual, so I dined on simple soup and bread. I think of you and the boys, and the quiet of our home in Berlin. The noise here is tiresome.

Yours,
G.W.F. Hegel

Bad weather on Sunday afternoon. — Because I overlooked the note on the theater program: “Start exceptionally /67 o’clock,” I only went at 7 o’clock and just missed the main thing: the chorus “Long live our good Emperor Franz”; — then the first act of Zelmira, how Dardanelli sang divinely! and above all Donzelli a recitative, which was his triumph! in opera seria he is unsurpassed, — he and Lablache — bearded with black curls, what antique heads!

My dearest Marie,

The air in Vienna is thick with autumn, but my spirits remain high. I wandered the Prater this afternoon; it is a magnificent spectacle of light and life, though I confess I grew weary of the crowds and sought refuge in the Leopoldstadt theatre.

We attended a prelude featuring Schuster. He plays an elderly merchant with a young wife to perfection—there is a certain ironic wisdom in the character that resonates deeply with the human condition. We then watched *Die Zauberbirn* again. The magic is charming, of course, but it is the interplay of human will and circumstance that truly engages the intellect.

I think of you constantly. The distance feels great, yet our minds remain close. I shall send word soon.

Your affectionate,
G.W.F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

The air in Vienna is thick with the smell of roasted chestnuts and indifference. We spent the afternoon in the Prater; the crowds were immense, but the rides were dull. I paid two Gulden for a carriage that shook my teeth loose.

Dinner was late, at the old tavern near the Ring. The soup was cold, but the wine was a decent Zweigelt. I met Schuster afterward. He is a large man, loud as a trumpet, and claims his new role in *Die Zauberbirn* makes him the king of the stage. I suspect he is merely the loudest. I attended the performance tonight. The prelude was tedious, but Schuster’s merchant was surprisingly alive. The young wife, however, looked as if she wished to be anywhere else.

I miss the quiet of our study. The heat here makes thinking difficult. I have bought a new coat; the tailor overcharged me, but the fabric is fine.

Yours,
G.W.F.

After the Prater, to the Leopoldstadt Theatre; here a prelude, in which Schuster, almost in the same manner as the older merchant with a young woman, as before, and then once again the Magic Pear; if only I could have had the young ones with me, — you yourself would not have been too old to amuse yourself a second time with it, as was my case.

My dearest Marie,

I return to my lodgings in Vienna with a mind full of impressions. I spent the morning until noon at Prince Lichtenstein’s gallery, marveling at the collection, before journeying to Währing to visit Rembold, the local professor of philosophy. It is always good to find a kindred spirit in these provinces.

After crossing an arm of the Danube, I took lunch in the Augarten and walked through the Prater. The air is pleasant, though the heat remains. I concluded the day at the Leopoldstadt theatre. Schuster’s performance as the Magister was amusing, and we finished with *Die Zauberbirn*. I confess I enjoyed the evening immensely.

I think of you and the boys constantly. The distance feels vast, yet my heart remains in Berlin. I trust your health is good and that the house is at peace. I shall write again soon.

Your loving husband,
Hegel

My dearest Marie,

The heat in Vienna is a trial. I spent the morning at Prince Lichtenstein’s gallery until noon, where the light was better than the crowd. Then I took the carriage to Währing, half an hour out, to see Rembold. He is a decent man, though his philosophy is mostly dust. We crossed the Danube arm to lunch in the Augarten. The fish was acceptable, costing me two florins, but the wine was thin.

I walked the Prater, which is merely trees and noise, then caught the Leopoldstadt theatre. Schuster played the Magister; he is loud and wooden. The farce, *Die Zauberbirn*, followed. It was vulgar, but the audience loved it. I paid a gulden for the seat.

Karl’s letter arrived yesterday; he is well, though his arithmetic remains slow. I shall send the books I promised when I return.

Your affectionate,
G.W.F.

At present I still feel yesterday in my bones, for it was a day of hard marching. — After the writing lesson I had with you — I mean, without having first called on you, I could not go out — I went first once more to the Princely Liechtenstein Gallery; — if I were to go there ten more times, I would not exhaust its treasures; — stood in it until 12 o'clock, — then to Währing, — that gallery is nearly half an hour away, — from there, — to visit my colleague, the Professor of the local Chair of Philosophy, Rembold — not as old as I am, a proper fellow countryman of mine, to whom my writings are not unknown), — only the people here] all stay too much cooped up, — traveling and getting about does not come so easily to them as to us. — From there I crossed a branch of the Danube and went to the Augarten for lunch, — never so tasty and so cheap as in my inn, where the fatal carriage meal takes place, and ate with a good appetite; afterwards I looked around in the Augarten. The garden is maintained just like the one in Schönbrunn, — broad, grand avenues, — the trees, shrubs in the paths cut into vertical flat walls, the trees like fans, or as if you left the stem on a pear and cut it into a disc on it, about as thick as the stem is, — so that one walks only between trees, not under trees and foliage, and always has the sky, which today was indeed so beautifully blue, above one's head; also the sun is already lower, so there is shade from the walls. — But at the end of the Augarten there is a view of the richest countryside, which has the hills about an hour away — Leopoldsberg, Kahlenberg — as its boundary, — in the most beautiful light the most beautiful landscape! — For such spots we are to be envied here. — Afterwards to the Prater — a forest, as I love it, with green grass, without any undergrowth and bushes between the tree trunks; — besides an innumerable number of taverns, bowling greens, carousels, optical room travels etc., I found some very elegant coffee pavilions here one writes correctly Kaffeh) — finally, after long wandering about, out of fatigue, to rest, to the Leopoldstadt Theatre, where Schuster played a Magister quite excellently, otherwise spoke High German; the second was again the Magic Pear, and went, very tired, in the most beautiful moonlight, — the fine weather is unchangeably faithful — home and to supper

My dearest Marie,

I am safe in Dresden, having arrived last evening after a pleasant stop in Töplitz. The journey was swift, and the weather kind enough to spare us the worst of the autumn chill.

I dropped into Tiek’s for a moment of respite and found Professor Hinrichs, who is now bound for Halle. We exchanged pleasantries over wine, his departure a small loss to the academic circle. I also sat with a gentleman who spoke with great vehemence about poetry and history. I had no idea who he was until he departed, at which point I realized it was Friedrich von Schlegel. He is a man of considerable energy, though his views seem to wander far from the solid ground of systematic thought. I suspect he has not yet settled his mind, but I found the conversation stimulating enough to wake me from the travel fatigue.

I shall rest now. Do not worry; I am well, and I miss you and the boys terribly.

Your devoted
G.W.F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

I write from Dresden, where I arrived yesterday evening after a tiring day in Töplitz. The journey is tedious, but the company here is better. I took dinner at Tiek’s and found myself in conversation with Professor Hinrichs, who is moving to Halle. He speaks well, but one senses the restlessness of a man uprooting himself. He left before I could ask him about the new chair, and I suspect he is more interested in his own departure than in the position.

Schlegel was there as well. I did not know who he was until after he had gone. I heard he is a man of some reputation in the Romantic circle, but I confess I have little patience for those who turn philosophy into poetry. It is a pleasant confusion, I suppose, to meet a famous name only to realize you have missed the man.

The food was decent, the wine passable. I paid too much for the room, as is my custom. I hope the boys are well and that Ludwig is not causing trouble. I shall continue on to Vienna in a few days.

Yours,
G.W.F.

P.S. Dresden, October 11, 1824. Arrived in Töplitz on Saturday afternoon, and from there came here yesterday evening — so far, or rather so near, am I to you, my dearest. Last evening I went immediately to Tiek’s and there encountered Professor Hinrichs in the midst of his move to Halle, along with Mr. Friedrich von Schlegel, who was only introduced to me after he had left.

My dearest Marie,

The basin here is vast, three to four hours wide, wedged between the mountain ranges that separate Saxony from Bohemia. From the Schloßberg, the view is commanding, stretching all the way to Aussig on the Elbe. I walked the town today, observing the flow of people with the usual curiosity.

In the evening, I attended the theatre. I confess, I was somewhat bored by *Preciosa*. The plot felt thin, and the acting lacked the necessary gravity. I found myself wondering if the audience would agree, or if they are simply content with pleasant distraction. It reminded me of our conversations here in Berlin; sometimes the public demands only entertainment, not depth.

The air is sharp, and the walk did me good. I miss the warmth of our home and the sound of the boys. Tell me how Karl and Immanuel fare in their studies. I hope they are applying themselves with the requisite discipline, rather than merely chasing amusement.

Yours,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

The Töplitz basin, some three hours wide, stretched out before me today from the Schloßberg, a vast amphitheater between the Saxon and Bohemian ranges. Kulm and Marienschein sat quietly on the horizon, with Aussig far off on the Elbe. The air is sharp here, cutting away the Berlin damp.

I strolled the town and, after a modest dinner of roast duck and local wine, attended a performance of *Preciosa*. The acting was wooden, the costumes threadbare; I paid two florins for the privilege of watching talent struggle against its own limitations. I found the audience, however, far more interesting than the stage, their faces reflecting a local pride that seems well-founded in their geography.

Karl’s last letter mentioned the autumn leaves; I see no such romance here, only the clear, cold logic of the mountains. I miss your snuff.

Your G.W.F.

Willdros, in the evening, and specifically Sunday evening). To continue the account! From the Castle Hill there is a view over the entire valley of Töplitz — a valley between two mountain ranges — one being the mountains that separate Saxony from Bohemia, and a second range to the south of it, between which lies a valley three to four hours wide — Töplitz in the middle — the Nollendorf Church on the height, Kulm, Marienschein (you are meant by this), at the foot of the first range — Aussig lies in the corner by the Elbe, between the range towards the east — (the boys should look at the map of the Seven Years' War). Then I still took a walk around Töplitz — finally went to the theatre, a few acts of Preciosa — an even more delicate Zierlisel than the one you so titled in Berlin.

My dearest Marie,

I am writing from Duxan, having stopped for the night. The road here is quiet, and the evening air is cool enough to make a man appreciate the warmth of our own parlor, where you are keeping the hearth bright for my return. I have been thinking of the little ones; do tell me how Karl and Immanuel fared this week, and that Ludwig is not causing too much mischief in the study.

The journey is steady, though the miles seem to stretch when one is away from familiar faces. I do miss our evening conversations, and the simple pleasure of a shared meal without the distraction of postillions and inns. I shall reach Töplitz by morning, I hope, where I intend to spend a day in rest before continuing. Do not worry over my health; I am as robust as ever, though perhaps a little stiff in the joints from the carriage.

Give my love to all.

Yours ever,
G.W.F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

The carriage rattled us to Duxan by four, half-way to Töplitz. The innkeeper, a stout Bohemian named Kral, insisted we stay, citing the mist closing in over the Elbe. He was right; the view from the window is grey and flat, a perfect mirror of my mood after eating cold mutton. The wine is thin, but the snuff is excellent. I paid three florins for the room and dinner; a fair price for the dust.

Karl’s letter reached me in Prague. I see he has begun his studies. Tell him to listen to his instructors, not his own cleverness. Obedience is the soil in which judgment grows. Do not let Ludwig linger too long at the café; I want him walking with me tomorrow.

The mist is thickening. I will sleep soon. Kiss the boys for me.

Your
G.W.F.

You probably hardly know where Duxan is in the world; I myself have only known it for half an hour; I will share my knowledge with you as well. Duxan lies a little more than halfway on the road from Prague to Töplitz, and I am spending the night here.

My dearest Marie,

I have been in the Emperor’s greenhouses by the Burg. It is a remarkable place, though the air is close and heavy, quite unlike the crisp evening here. I entered and left through an underground passage that the Emperor uses daily for his afternoon walks. It struck me as a curious little mechanism of power: the sovereign moving through the earth, hidden from the world, while his subjects gaze at the leaves above. It is a physical symbol of how the state operates—often unseen, yet structuring everything we see.

I am tired now, but my spirits are good. The light in this city has a particular quality tonight; it feels less like the grey fog of Berlin and more like a promise. I think of you and the boys, and how strange it is to be so far from the familiar. I will rest soon, but I shall write again when we move on.

Your affectionate husband,
G.W.F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

The air in the Burg greenhouses is thick with the scent of orange blossoms, a sharp contrast to the stale study air in Berlin. I walked the Emperor’s private path today, entering through an underground passage he uses for his afternoon retreats. It is a curious thing, to walk in the footsteps of absolute power while smelling damp earth and rotting fruit. I paid six kreuzer for a bottle of water and a small cake, which was dry and tasteless.

I met a young professor from Prague, eager to discuss Fries. I told him plainly that his system is a house of cards; he looked pale, then left. I am tired from the walk and the heat. The light here is yellow, unlike our clear blue. I hope Karl’s health is steady. I shall write again from Brno. Give my regards to Immanuel.

Yours,
G.W.F.

Greenhouses by the Castle, went in and out through a kind of underground passage, through which the Emperor goes every day, and spends some afternoon hours in his gardens. — But the bloom — I could only hope for georginas and altheas — quite insignificant, — that is quite different on the Peacock Island.

My dearest Marie,

The Parisian theatre is a curious mix of brilliance and tedium. I passed Pesaroni tonight; his reputation was too loud, and I would not waste an evening on mere noise. Instead, we attended the English company at the Odeon. The language was strange in my ears, but the actors possessed a certain raw, unpolished energy that the Italians lack. I have already seen Mlle Mars in *Emilia*. She is a force of nature, though perhaps too intense for my taste.

I find myself thinking of you and the boys. Berlin feels distant, yet the longing for home is a constant companion in these foreign streets. I am tired, but the journey continues. I hope the weather has been kind to the garden.

Your loving
Georg

My dearest Marie,

The English company at the Odeon was a necessary refuge. Pesaroni sings, but tonight the air here demanded something else, and the theatre near my lodgings obliged. The actors were adequate; the scenery, as usual in Paris, a bit of painted cardboard. I paid two francs for a seat that smelled of damp wool.

We saw Mlle Mars earlier in *Emilia*. She is still formidable, though her voice has thinned. It is interesting to watch how the public swallows her gestures as if they were logical proofs. One sees the spirit of the age in their applause.

I am well. The wine in the Rhineland was better than anything I have found here. Do tell the boys to mind their conduct at the Gymnasium; obedience is the only foundation that holds.

I shall sleep late tomorrow.

Yours ever,
G.W.F. Hegel

I have not been to the French theatre as much as I had thought; the small theatres and plays are pleasant, but I am soon done with them; they are jokes that one quickly gets over. Mlle Mars is currently playing only in *Emilia*, in which I saw her. The Pesaroni sang yesterday, but we preferred the English, who are in my neighbourhood (Odeon).

My dearest Marie,

I am writing from Brussels, where the evening air is cool after a long day’s travel. I dined at the house of Mr. van Ghert, a man of considerable standing. His household is lively—five boys and a daughter, the eldest now seventeen. They were most gracious, sending their warmest regards to you.

The father spoke with great hope of Berlin. He intends to send his eldest son here in some four years to complete his studies. It is a fine arrangement; the boy has a steady mind, and Berlin offers the proper discipline for his final formation. I promised to keep his name in mind, that he might find a place in my circle of instruction.

The journey continues, but my spirits are good. I have taken my snuff and rested my eyes. Do not worry for me; I am well cared for.

Your faithful
Georg

My dearest Marie,

I have just left the van Ghert house, where I sat at table with six children—five boys, one girl. The eldest, seventeen, is to come to Berlin in four years to complete his studies. They sent their warmest regards to you; I promised them the door would be open. A fine, bustling family. The wine was passable, though the roast beef was a trifle dry. I paid the usual modest sum for the evening’s hospitality.

I walked back through the dark streets, thinking how strange it is to be a guest in another’s domestic sphere, observing the quiet machinery of a household while the world turns outside. It reminds one that the state is not merely an abstraction but a web of such particular lives.

I am tired but content. The air here is cool. Do tell Karl I saw a boy who might do well with his geometry.

Your affectionate
G.W.F. Hegel

Farewell — in 4 years perhaps we shall see Mr. v. Gh. and his wife in Berlin, who have asked us to recommend them to you in the best possible way, and to grant us the permission to make that promise; we are sitting at the table with 6 children, 5 boys and 1 girl; the eldest son is 17 years old, — when he has completed his studies here, he is to complete them in Berlin, in reliance on us.

My dearest Marie,

We have reached Weimar, and the air here is thick with the scent of damp earth and history. I am lodging near Goethe, who receives me with the warmth I have long hoped for. This evening, the Grand Duke joined us for tea. I sat beside him on the sofa, and we conversed until nearly ten. It is a profound pleasure to speak with men of such stature, yet I confess my mind is already turning back to our quiet rooms in Berlin.

Tomorrow, Zelter and I shall ride in Goethe’s carriage to the Grand Duke’s botanical garden at Belvedere. I imagine the plants will be more orderly than the human soul, which is a comfort. The journey has been tiring, but the company, stimulating. I hope the house is comfortable in my absence. Kiss the boys for me, especially little Ludwig, who misses his father’s sharp tongue.

Yours,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

We arrived in Weimar at sunset, and I was straight away at Goethe’s. Riemer and Zelter were there, and the Grand Duke joined us for tea half an hour later. We sat together on the sofa and talked until nearly ten. It was a pleasant evening, though I confess my back aches from the carriage ride.

This morning, Zelter and I took Goethe’s carriage to the Grand Duke’s botanical garden at Belvedere. The collection is impressive, though the light was rather harsh for my eyes. We ate a simple lunch; the bread was good, the wine mediocre, and I paid six thalers for the pleasure. Goethe is still sharp, if a bit tired. The Grand Duke is affable but speaks in circles. I hope this letter finds you and the boys well. I have little else to report.

Your husband,
G.W.F. Hegel

My last letter had brought me as far as Elberfeld; from there it went straight across Westphalia via Arnsberg and Arolsen to Kassel. From Arnsberg, instead of a fast mail, an ordinary old post wagon departed, and it was the last one—the next time it would be an express wagon—I had to endure that last one; my hope of still going to Eisenach on Sunday could therefore not be fulfilled; I had to spend the night in Cassel, where we arrived only in the afternoon, rested, went to the theater for half an hour—Goethe’s Egmont—and only yesterday, on Monday, drove to Eisenach with a hired coachman—through forest valleys, a country not exactly pleasant. What we saw of Westphalia, the Wupper valley, then other valleys, the area around Arnsberg was more charming. Here I was no longer in France nor in the beautiful Netherlands, neither as to the regions nor the inns; the latter I noticed because of the good appetite I have; partly because for a few days there have been no good ones to be had, and partly because the coachmen led me to those that in their opinion or according to their interest were good, i.e., bad. I spent the night in Eisenach; in the morning before daybreak, so that I saw nothing of the town (for I had arrived at night), I drove out with a single-horse carriage in thick fog, which was only conquered by the sun towards Gotha; now it went in fine weather, from friendly Gotha to Erfurt, where I sought out Mr. v. Griesheim, but did not find him, though I met his brother, and paid my compliments to his mother, a truly dear, cultivated, and intelligent lady, who was not unknown to me. In the evening—with the setting sun—I then arrived here yesterday. So, after some arranging, I proceeded to the goal of this detour—the old revered friend. The house was illuminated; the Grand Duke had announced himself for tea; however, I had my arrival reported for the time being. Goethe received me in the friendliest and most heartfelt manner; I had many things to tell him; after half an hour the old Grand Duke came;—but I must still add a main point—that I found Zelter with Goethe besides Riemer. Goethe presented me to the gracious Lord, to whom I set myself on the sofa—I believe I even sat to his right—he asked about Paris—he is somewhat deaf. So the evening passed (Zelter and Riemer wisely sat in the adjoining room) as well as it could with the old gentleman, in conversation, until half past ten o’clock. Goethe stood by the whole time; I gradually noticed that the gentleman was somewhat deaf, and that when it became quiet with speaking, one should not try to entertain him, but wait until something occurs to him again—otherwise everything went quite unembarrassed; I had to endure being nailed to my sofa for a couple of hours. The Grand Duke had recommended that I see his botanical garden in Belvedere; I drove with Zelter this morning—Goethe had had his carriage ready for it—at ten o’clock out; they are in fact very large, extensive grounds; the Duke is himself a great botanist—there are beautiful specimens of plants to be seen there—we two were of course not connoisseurs enough to properly appreciate everything—we were back here at noon; I paid my visit to Mr. and Mrs. v. Schwendler, where I naturally heard much regret that you are not there and that I am separated from Goethe in

My dearest Marie,

I am writing from Trier, where the heat has been oppressive since my arrival yesterday. The city is a curiosity rather than a wonder; the ruins are merely stones, yet they remind one that freedom is not built in a day. I spent the morning walking with the innkeeper’s brother, who showed me the old Roman walls and an estate belonging to a relation of Eichhorn. It is strange to see such grandeur decayed, much like the old world order we are leaving behind.

In the afternoon, I visited the churches. There is a solemnity here that contrasts sharply with the bustle of Berlin. I am well, though tired from the journey. I think of you and the boys constantly. The journey to France continues tomorrow. I hope this letter finds you in good health.

Yours ever,
G. W. F. H.

My dearest Marie,

I am exhausted, having driven sixteen German miles from the previous night’s post to reach Trier by eight this morning. The heat was stifling. From eight until half-past one, the innkeeper’s brother, a man of little conversation but decent company, showed me the Roman ruins and the surrounding countryside. We visited an estate belonging to the Procurator-General Eichhorn’s brother-in-law; the grounds are respectable, though the house itself is merely adequate. I dined on a heavy local fare and paid a reasonable sum, though the wine was slightly acidic.

In the afternoon, I walked the churches. The stone here bears the weight of centuries, a silent witness to the progress of consciousness, though I suspect you would find my weariness more interesting than my musings on masonry. I have no news for the boys save that I am well and eating sufficiently.

I must rest. The journey continues tomorrow.

Your affectionate husband,
G.W.F.

Yesterday I had to get up at 3 o’clock in the morning in order to depart precisely at 4 o’clock by the express post for here; the journey is over 16 miles, very frequently just up hill, down hill, but on a fine carriage road; at 8 o’clock we were here. — I find everywhere people whom I know, and who are otherwise obliging and friendly. After I had slept well, I set out on my way after 8 o’clock, under the guidance of a brother of the innkeeper, who showed me the remarkable Roman ruins and took me around the area, among other things to an estate of the brother-in-law of the General Prosecutor Eichhorn; we were on our feet until 11½ o’clock. — Trier has an excellent location on the Moselle, a beautiful valley of the greatest fertility, bounded by gentle vineyards. — In the afternoon I was in the churches.

My dearest Marie,

I arrived in Paris this morning, having left my things at Cousin’s house to save the trouble of unpacking in a hotel. We are still hunting for a proper furnished room, but for now, we have settled into a routine of work and brief meals. At eleven, Cousin and I shared cutlets and a bottle of wine. It was a simple repast, but the wine was good, and the conversation lively. He is eager to see my letters to the post by two, so I must finish this note quickly. The streets here are busy, but I find a certain calm in the intellectual exchange. I am well, though the heat is oppressive. I think of you and the boys often. Do keep Ludwig’s studies steady; I trust you are managing the household well in my absence. I shall write again when I have secured a more permanent lodging.

Your loving,
G.W.F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

The heat in Paris is oppressive, though the air is thick with the scent of frying onions from the street stalls. This morning we moved out of the Hôtel des Princes, leaving our baggage at Cousin’s, a man of great intellect but little practical sense. We spent the hours hunting for a *chambre garnie*, a task more tedious than deciphering the *Geist*. Finally, at 11, we settled for a modest room near the Seine. Cousin insisted on a brief breakfast: cutlets, decent but heavy, and a bottle of good Burgundy. He is frantic to get my letter to the post by two, fearing the mail coaches have already departed.

I am tired. The dust here is worse than in the Rhineland. Tell the boys to mind their conduct; I expect them to be orderly, not merely happy.

Your husband,
G.W.F.

This morning I moved out of the Hotel des Princes and provisionally left the effects with my friend Cousin—it is very expensive there—this morning we will find a furnished room. That we are well together, in heartfelt cordiality, goes without saying—we did not linger long at breakfast (i.e., at 11 o'clock we ate cutlets and drank a bottle of wine) because he has to look after the interests of Mrs. Hegel, i.e., to see to it that this letter gets to the post office today, which must be by 2 o'clock...

My dearest Marie,

I write from Paris, where I arrived this morning. The heat is oppressive, and the city feels like a living beast, breathing in the streets. I have secured a room at the Hôtel des Princes, a respectable establishment, though the dust is already settling on my coat.

I paid my respects to Cousin immediately; he is still vigorous, if somewhat lost in his own system. I spent the afternoon wandering the Boulevards and the Palais Royal. The crowds are immense, a chaotic mix of commerce and idleness. I walked the Champs Élysées this evening, past the cafés and carousels, where families gather in the fading light. It is a spectacle of pure sensuous life, lacking the quiet dignity I find in our home. I miss the silence of Berlin and the comfort of your company. Pray tell the boys their father thinks of them.

Yours,
G.W.F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

I am settled at the Hôtel des Princes, a decent enough room for the price, though the air is thick. I saw Cousin this evening; he is still chattering about "spirit" as if he had invented it, which is amusing given our own work. We walked the Boulevards later. The Palais Royal is a labyrinth of small shops, and the Tuileries were quiet. But the Champs Élysées! It is a spectacle. The Ambassadeurs and Aurore are packed with families, children spinning on carousels, coffee being drunk in great quantities. It feels less like a city and more like a large, noisy market for the soul.

The food here is light; I ate a simple soup and some bread, perhaps too little. I am tired. The journey from Berlin has worn me down. I miss the stillness of our house and the sound of the boys’ voices. I shall rest now. Do not worry; I am well, just far away.

Your loving Georg

Here, between 10 and 11 o'clock on Sunday, having arrived yesterday, I took up quarters at the Hôtel des Princes, — and immediately sought out my cousin. — But here I am overwhelmed by the multitude of great sights I have already seen and traversed, that is to say, from the outside. The Boulevards, the Palais Royal, the Louvre, the Tuileries, the Luxembourg, the Garden and Palace, and so on. — Last evening the Champs Elysées, where the Carousel is, and the taverns, that is to say, the coffee houses, namely those of the Ambassadeur and of the Aurore, — a state of affairs like at the tents, — only ten times more people at the tables, philistines with wives and children, and so forth. — When I walk through the streets, the people look exactly as they do in Berlin, — all dressed in the same way, roughly the same faces, — the same appearance, but in a populous mass.

My dearest Marie,

I write from my room in Brussels, the city’s quiet pressing in on me even as I wait for Cousin to join me for a walk. The diligence was swift; I arrived at six and, after a brief rest and breakfast, found your letter on my table. It was a true comfort to see your hand again after the journey’s monotony.

I am set to depart for Cologne tomorrow morning. I expect your next letter to be waiting for me there, so do not let the days slip by without telling me of the household and the boys. I find myself thinking of our Berlin evenings, of the cards and the conversation, with a sharpness that travel only deepens. The road is long, but my heart is steady knowing you are there.

Pray write soon. I am well, though weary, and eager to continue.

Yours forever,
G.W.F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

I write from my room in Brussels, having just finished dinner. The food was competent, if lacking the warmth of home, and I paid four francs for the meal, which I consider fair given the service. I spent the morning resting after the diligence, which was a wretched affair; the driver drove as if he were fleeing a ghost, and my back is still complaining.

I met Cousin this afternoon. He is as lively as ever, though his talk of philosophy grew tedious after the first hour. We walked the streets and looked at the shops. I must confess, the tailors here are inferior to those in Berlin, but I found a decent cravat.

I depart for Cologne tomorrow morning. Do ensure my letter regarding the accounts is waiting for me there, as I need to settle the matter with the publisher. I hope the journey will be less turbulent.

Your affectionate,
G.W.F.

Yesterday afternoon at 3 o’clock I got back into the coach, on which I arrived here this morning at 6 o’clock, then went to bed, had breakfast, and, upon receiving your letter, wrote quickly, in order now to go out with my dear friend and cousin. — Tomorrow morning we continue — to Cölln, where I await a letter from you.

My dearest Marie,

I must ask you to stop worrying so. The letter from Immanuel, asking after my health, arrived with yours. I am quite well. It was merely a slight fever, the sort one often catches when changing climates, and it has already broken. I have been walking in the gardens here; the air is fresh, and my spirits are high.

Please do not let anxiety take hold of you or the boys. I am not a fragile thing to be handled with tweezers. I am still the same Hegel who walked into Napoleon’s camp at Jena. A little rest in Paris will do me more good than medicine. I shall take care of myself, as I always do, and return to Berlin when my work here is finished.

Write to me of the household, of the little ones, but keep your worries to yourself. I need your letters to be a comfort, not a report of distress.

Yours always,
G.W.F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

You write of my illness with such alarm, and Immanuel asks what caused it? It was merely the damp cold and a bad digestion, nothing more. I am well now.

I spent the morning with Cousin. He is a clever man, though he talks too much about "spirit" without having read the *Phenomenology*. He insisted on paying for my dinner at the Café de Paris—four francs for a mediocre soup and a glass of claret. I let him, as it is a fine way to settle accounts. The wine was ordinary, but the company was livelier than usual.

I walked the Tuileries in the late afternoon. The light on the Seine was quite beautiful, but the crowds are thick with tourists. I bought a small snuff box for two francs to replace the one I lost in Berlin.

I am not ill, only tired. Tell Karl to stop worrying so much, or he will be the next one to fall.

Your loving husband,
G.W.F.

After returning from this excursion, Cousin gave me your kind letter, in which you write to me about my ill health and your worries about it. Immanuel writes, what caused me to become unwell? — he must know that I am no longer such a small springing-about fellow as he, but already an old father, — that I wish for advanced age and health, especially in order to see him and his brother continue to flourish, and to be able to contribute my part to it, — and to be able to share with you, my dear, for a long time yet, this satisfaction which is to be hoped for and which was brought into fresher remembrance on his birthday...

My dearest Marie,

The Rhine at Cologne is a different beast from the stream near Berlin. The river is wide, grey, and swollen with commerce. I counted twelve large two-masted vessels today, each one a testament to the practical spirit of the West. I walked the streets, the air thick with the smell of fish and coal smoke.

I visited the cathedral; the interior is impressive, though the light is gloomy. I am to attend mass tomorrow morning with the young Counts Stolberg and their tutor, Dean Kellermann. Kellermann speaks with the confidence of a man who has never been contradicted. He believes the constitution grows from the soil, not from Parisian pamphlets. I am to leave for Aachen this afternoon. The innkeeper charged me two thalers for a room that smells of damp wool and yesterday’s onions.

I hope Karl is doing well in his studies. Obedience is the first lesson; I miss seeing him learn to listen before he speaks.

Your affectionate,
G.W.F.H.

My dearest Marie,

I reached Amsterdam at noon, straight to Dr. Besseling, who was gracious but busy. The food at his table was competent, if dull; I paid two guilders for the meal. Later I wandered into the picture gallery. I must confess I was struck dumb by a Rembrandt, some fifteen feet wide. It is not merely a picture; it is the very air of the city. I did not finish the collection, nor do I wish to. My eyes are tired, and the light here is flat compared to Berlin’s.

I think of the boys. I hope they are studying, not just idling. I have taken a room near the canal; the noise of the water is constant, a kind of restlessness. I am tired, but content. Write to me soon.

Yours,
G.W.F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

The day was long, but the company in Giessen was excellent. We drank local wine with the professors; I find their arguments as dry as their cellar, but their hospitality is warm. The travelers for Frankfurt departed, leaving me with a Jewish schoolmaster, a man of surprising wit and good taste. We walked the Lahn past Weilburg. The old princely residence looks neglected, a fine ruin. I paid four Kreuzer for a simple meal at a wayside inn; the bread was stale, but the river air was crisp. I am tired, but the walk did me good. I think of Karl and Immanuel only in the sense that I hope your health is steady. Do not worry about my expenses; I am managing well. The light on the water this evening was quite striking, though I have no time to paint it. I shall write again tomorrow if the post allows.

Yours,
G.W.F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

I reached Kassel at eleven, sharp as a pin. The air is cool after the heat of the Rhineland, and my legs are thanking me for the walk through the old town. The architecture is heavy, but the gardens are superb. I spent the afternoon wandering the Herkules, though I confess the statues are a bit overwrought; I paid two thalers for the guide, which was a waste, as I know the history of the place better than he does.

Dinner was unremarkable—thin broth, cold meat. I paid four thalers for the room, which is dear for the quality. I am tired, but my mind is clear. I miss the smell of our library in Berlin and the sound of the boys’ laughter. Write to me soon, and tell me how the servants managed in my absence. I shall travel to Frankfurt tomorrow, if the weather holds.

Your affectionate,
Georg

My dearest Marie,

The heat was dreadful today. I sat facing backwards in the Kassel coach, a position that suits a man of my age, allowing me to observe the world receding while I watch my own face age in the glass. My companion, a Göttingen student, clutched the rear seat number one with the tenacity of a man defending a state’s constitution, refusing to yield an inch to the other passengers. It is a small, petty form of freedom, but I admire the stubbornness.

We followed the Lahn river, the water dark and sluggish under the sun. The food at the inn was thin broth and stale bread, but the wine was passable. I have sent for a change of shirts; the travel dust is becoming a nuisance. I do not know if you received my last letter regarding the printing proofs, but I suspect the typesetter is as slow as the river.

I am tired but content. Do not worry.

Your affectionate
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

The rain in the Rhine passenger boat this morning was miserable, but the view saved it. At Linz I visited the hilltop church Schulze recommended; the painting is adequate, though the climb was stiff. In Bonn, Windischmann and his son-in-law Walther were most agreeable. Windischmann is sharp, but Walther lacks that certain *Geist* I expect in a lawyer. We drank decent wine, though the price was steep.

I am tired. The journey from Koblenz to here has worn me thin. I hope Karl and Immanuel are well, and that Ludwig is not giving the servants trouble with his temper. Tell me how the house is settled. I shall take a short walk tomorrow if the sky clears, but for now, I am exhausted.

Yours ever,
Hegel

My dearest Marie,

I arrived in Breda just as the light was failing, having taken the evening coach from here. The air was cool, a relief after the Dutch heat. I was shown a tomb monument here, ascribed to Michelangelo, though I suspect the attribution is more wishful thinking than fact. It features a count and his wife in alabaster on a black slab, supported by four standing figures at the corners: Julius Caesar, Hannibal, and Regulus. It is a curious mix of pagan virtue and domestic repose. The composition feels heavy, the stone dark, yet there is a quiet dignity to the dead couple that surpasses the stiff, heroic posturing of the living figures above them. I paid the keeper two guilders to see it, which I think was fair.

I am tired. The food in the coach was mediocre, but the wine passable. I hope the boys are behaving themselves in Berlin. Write to me soon.

Your loving,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

The coach was comfortable, though the roads from Aachen to here were muddy. In Aachen I spent the entire morning and afternoon at Bettendorf’s house. He is a man of good taste and no small fortune; his collection of paintings is superb, far superior to what we see in the provincial galleries of Germany. I sat in Charlemagne’s actual coronation chair while the sexton explained the mechanics of the old empire. It is a strange sensation to sit in the seat of such power, feeling the weight of history not as abstraction, but as wood and leather.

I then walked to Burtscheid and took a sulphur bath. It was hot and unpleasant, but I confess it loosened my joints, which have been stiff from the journey. I dined at the inn; the food was plain, but the wine was decent. I have paid all bills and am ready to continue.

How are the boys? I trust Immanuel is not neglecting his Latin. I am well, if tired.

Your
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

The rain has drowned the illuminations for the Emperor’s name day, but the house at the Italian opera was thick as a crowd. Twenty-nine voices, including Fodor and Rubini, sang the anthem in unison. It was loud, certainly, though I confess the German premiere of the Auber work that followed was a trifle stiff. I met a friend who insists the food in the foyer is inferior to our Berlin dining, a claim I am not yet prepared to concede.

I have sent my luggage on ahead. It is strange to be so light; one feels less anchored, perhaps more like a thought in motion rather than a substance. I hope Karl is managing his studies with the requisite discipline, and not letting his imagination wander too far ahead of his logic. I shall write again from Prague.

Your loving
Hegel

My dearest Marie,

The Italian company is here, and the air in the opera house is thick with perfumes and tobacco. We took our seats near the stage, thanks to the Kleins who extended their stay just to sit with us. Lablache’s Figaro is a marvel of agility, though Dardanelli’s Countess sings with a sweetness that makes one forget her lack of power. Donzelli is adequate. The music is still the same, but the execution is sharper.

We dined at the Hofkeller. The wine was cold and the bread stale, but the company was good. I paid a small fortune for the ticket, which I regret, but I am glad I came.

Karl writes that his health is improving; I hope he is not overworking his eyes. The heat here is oppressive. I am tired.

Your loving husband,

G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

I am back in my room, exhausted but content. This morning I spent two hours in the Esterhazy gallery, a third visit, but I confess the private cabinet dazzled me. The valet was courteous, though perhaps too eager to point out every crack in the plaster. I saw the Rubens, which is indeed magnificent, but the lighting here is dim; I paid two florins for the privilege of seeing it poorly.

Lunch was with Sonnleitner and a Paduan professor. The wine was good, the roast pheasant excellent, and the conversation light. Sonnleitner is a solid man, if a bit dull on the subject of Roman law. We paid three guilders each, a fair sum for the heat.

In the evening I saw Rossini’s *Corradino*. The music is intoxicating, though the libretto drags in the second act. I nearly dozed off during the recitatives, but the chorus woke me. It is a spectacle, not a thought.

You asked about the snuff; I bought a tin of the finest brand here. It is strong. I miss your quiet, and the boys’ noise. I shall write more soon.

Yours,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

The fair weather finally broke this morning, and the Kleins have departed for their journey. We met at breakfast at 9, where I paid six Kreuzer for a decent roll and coffee. Their daughter is pleasant enough, though her father speaks with that distinct, nasal Viennese affectation that I find exhausting. We did little sightseeing together; we simply sat.

I walked alone to the Karlskirche this afternoon. The light was grey, but the architecture is imposing. I spent an hour there, thinking, as I often do, about how the stone must have been laid before the idea was fully formed. It is a strange tension, but the building holds.

I am tired. The hotel bed is stiff, and I paid two Florins for the privilege. I hope the children are well and that Ludwig is not disturbing your peace. I shall stay three more days to see the Prater.

Your loving
Georg

My dearest Marie,

The Belvedere in the afternoon was tolerable, though the crowds were thick. At six, I joined the Partheys for the *Barber of Seville*. Lablache as Figaro is indeed spirited, though Fodor’s Rosina lacks breath. The audience clapped until the singers returned three times; I confess I found the repetition tedious, but the Partheys, at my urging, were enchanted. We paid two florins for the seats, a fair price for the noise. Dinner at the tavern was mediocre, and I have already complained to the waiter about the wine. I read the theatre paper’s notice, which praises the newcomer de Franco highly. I am tired. Kiss the boys for me, and tell Karl he must stop writing such long letters.

Your devoted
G.W.F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

The rain here has been a veritable deluge, soaking the city from Sunday into today. Yet I insisted on the carriage to the Augarten, and thence to Nussdorf, for a mind that sits still too long grows rust. The air is thick, but the walk was good.

Look at the enclosed petals. I stopped by a great pear tree on the road; the fruit was picked days ago, yet there it was, in full blossom again. It struck me as a strange defiance of the order of things, as if the tree had forgotten its own history. I picked two for you.

I dined at a small inn in Nussdorf. The wine was ordinary, the bread hard, but the company—two young men from the University—was lively. They spoke of the new laws with a certainty that borders on arrogance, but one has to listen to see where the spirit is turning.

Tell the boys the rain does not stop the world, only the lazy. I am tired, but content.

Your loving,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

The day began early at the Imperial Library. I spent the morning with Raphael and Marcantonio, paying the usual modest sum to the attendants. The light here is distinct from Berlin’s; one must tip well to be left in peace. The weather cleared by afternoon, so I walked.

I confess I am tired. The Viennese have a habit of lingering over meals that tests my patience. I dined on a simple soup and bread; it was adequate, if uninspired. I think of Karl’s lessons at home and the quiet of our study.

I saw a performance earlier, though I do not speak well of the dancers. Eberle was there, but the German school seems to lack the true spirit of movement. It is all form without life. I shall not return.

I write this by candlelight. The ink is thick, but my thoughts are clear. I am well, though the cold seeps in. Give my regards to the boys.

Yours,
G.W.F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

The heat here is oppressive, though the air is dry. Today I finished my surveys of the galleries. The lighting is poor, and the guides are tedious, but the works themselves are sufficient. At noon I dined with the von H. family. Their table was heavy, the wine flat, but they are polite enough. They drove us to the Pleasure Garden outside the city. I confess I have little patience for such public amusements; the crowds are thick and the music shrill. I sat in a shaded corner, ate a cold chicken, and paid two florins for the privilege of standing near a fountain.
