The uncle’s son spoke of politics with the confidence of a boy who has never had to pay for his opinions. I let him.

I hope the boys are behaving. I shall dine with them again tomorrow, then move on. Do not worry; I am well, if somewhat tired.

Your
G. W. F. H.

My dearest Marie,

Metz is grey and damp, though the Moselle from the ramparts is enough to make a man forget the sleet. I walked the perimeter before dinner; the cathedral is grand but cold from the outside. I dined at the *Hôtel de la Poste*—the duck was overcooked, the wine passable, and I paid six francs for the privilege of being cold.

In the evening, I attended the theatre. The house was full of garrison officers, loud and smelling of tobacco, which made the *vaudeville* a farce of noise. I watched them more than the play; a certain Colonel, red-faced and blustering, seemed to think his applause could alter the script. It was tiresome.

I have secured a front coupé seat for tomorrow’s diligence to Paris. It will be a long drive, and I shall need my snuff.

How are the boys? I trust Ludwig is behaving in his studies. I miss your quiet company and the smell of our library more than I care to admit.

Yours,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

The Paris heat is a beast, but the evening air on Montmartre was glorious. We visited the abattoirs today; a grim spectacle of industry, yet one must see the machinery of the city. We also inspected the Bourse and the Chamber of Deputies. The latter is grand, but I confess the former held more interest.

Dined at 5:30 with Cousin and Fauriel. Cousin is as brilliant and insufferable as ever; he speaks of history as if he invented it. Fauriel, the Greek song editor, is charming and ate with great enthusiasm. The food was excellent, the wine even better, and the bill, though stiff, was worth it for the conversation. Mignet and Thiers were absent, but their absence was felt.

I hope the boys are well and that Karl’s studies in logic are progressing without too much fuss. I miss your quiet, but the road is long.

Yours,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

The Parisians have finally given me a sleepwalker. Three acts, though only the first was actually danced; the rest was mere miming, a pantomime of the absurd. A man wandering roofs with a lantern? I confess I found it less terrifying than the price of the wine at Saint-Cloud yesterday. The Seine was calm, but the water charges a premium for its stillness. I ate a decent duck, though the service was slow, and I paid three francs for the privilege of being ignored by the waiter.

Ludwig is well, though he complains of the dust. I do not know if it is the air or the wine, but my head feels light, perhaps too light. The French seem to mistake motion for life. I am tired, Marie. Do not worry; I shall rest before dinner.

Yours,
Georg

My dearest Marie,

The day was warm, the dust thick. We drove with Raumer to Saint-Denis; the cathedral still hung in black for a recent funeral. A strange, heavy silence there. We pressed on to Montmorency. I took a donkey to the Hermitage, Rousseau’s old spot. The animal was stubborn, but the view from the heights was grand—Paris and Montmartre stretching out below like a map.

Raumer is talkative, full of French politics, but he listens well when I speak. We dined at a small inn; the wine was decent, the bread heavy. I paid five francs for the ride and supper. My legs ache, but the mind is clear.

You asked of the books I sent. They should be there by next week. Tell Karl his father thinks him too hasty in his essays on ethics; let him read more history. I miss your quiet room and the sound of the children.

I am tired. Sleep well.

Your G.W.F.H.

My dearest Marie,

I write from van Ghert’s house in Brussels, where Madame van Ghert performed the odd trick of cutting me a quill pen herself. The ink is good, but the nib bites. I had my letter from you fetched from the post office this morning; your news of Karl’s grammar exercises is received with approval, though I suspect his Latin declensions are still a battleground.

The city is busy, the coffee strong, and the air sharp. I walked the boulevards this afternoon; the light is golden, but the pavement is uneven. I dined on a simple stew and a glass of wine, paying four francs. It was honest food. I am tired, as you might expect, but my spirits are high. The journey continues tomorrow toward the Rhine.

Tell the boys I am thinking of them, and that their father is well enough to complain about the weather.

Your loving,
G.

My dearest Marie,

The journey from Brussels to Ghent was uneventful, save for the heat in the diligence. I spent the afternoon in Ghent viewing the Ghent Altarpiece panels. Van Eyck’s light is uncanny; it feels less like paint and more like a window into a different epoch. I arrived in Bruges by canal barge at 8 p.m. The cabin was cramped, filled with men playing whist with a fervor that bordered on the religious. I watched a hand for an hour; one player’s arrogance was positively comical, though his play was sound.

Dinner was adequate, if uninspiring. I paid three francs for a modest meal and a bottle of local wine. I am tired, and the barge rocked enough to unsettle my stomach. I think of you and the boys here in the quiet of this Flemish town. The air is damp. I hope Karl is studying diligently and Immanuel is not causing trouble. I shall write again when I reach Paris.

Yours always,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

The Rhine is a fine sight, though the heat is stifling. I reached Koblenz yesterday, took a bath to cool off, and have been writing to you since. The journey through Kassel with the Beers was pleasant enough; they are a decent sort, if a bit stiff. Marburg was a quick stop to see Suabedissen—he is older now, and his mind, while still sharp, moves with a certain slowness that reminds me of our own aging. In Wetzlar, Schulz’s wife made an excellent dinner. The wine was good, the bread fresh, and the conversation light. I paid two thalers for the coach to Koblenz, which I consider fair for the distance, though the driver was a fool who nearly lost a wheel on the cobblestones.

Karl and Immanuel must be in their studies. Tell them to keep their heads down and their spirits up. Ludwig is quiet, I hope. I am tired but content. The air here is thick, but the view from the castle is worth the climb.

Yours,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

The air in Paris is thick with dust and ambition. I spent the afternoon at the Louvre, walking the long halls with Raumer and Panofka. It is the last day before the gallery opens to the living painters, a strange inversion of value, but the old masters still hold the ground. The light in the afternoon was poor, but the shadows in the corners gave the canvases a certain depth that the midday sun strips away.

We dined at a small table near the Seine; the wine was acceptable, the service tedious. I paid four francs for a meal that offered little more than sustenance, though the view of the river was a fair compensation. I have read your last letter; Immanuel’s progress with his Latin is noted, though I fear his attention to detail is still lacking. A boy who does not master the small rules has no business claiming the large freedoms.

I am tired. I shall take my snuff and rest.

Your affectionate
G.W.F. Hegel
